Back: FTP Data channel. File transfer payload. Unencrypted. Exam trap: FTP uses two ports — 20 (data) and 21 (control). Replace with SFTP (port 22) or FTPS (port 990).

FTP Control channel. Command/authentication. Credentials sent in plaintext. Exam trap: FTP active mode sends data FROM server TO client on random port; passive uses server-range ports. Know FTP is insecure.
Secure Shell. Encrypted remote administration, file transfer (SFTP/SCP), port forwarding. Replaces Telnet (23). Exam trap: SSH uses TCP. SFTP is SSH-based, NOT related to FTP.
Unencrypted remote terminal. All data in cleartext. Exam trap: classic 'replace with SSH' answer. If a scenario says 'remote CLI access needed securely', answer is SSH (22), not Telnet.

Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. Server-to-server email. Unencrypted. Exam trap: port 25 is for MTA-to-MTA relay. Client submission uses port 587 (authenticated, STARTTLS). Blocking 25 prevents spam relay.

Cisco AAA protocol. Encrypts entire packet (unlike RADIUS which encrypts only password). Separates auth, authorization, accounting. TCP-based. Exam trap: TACACS+ is Cisco proprietary; RADIUS is IETF standard.
Domain Name System. UDP for queries (fast). TCP for zone transfers and responses >512 bytes. Exam trap: DNSSEC validates integrity (does NOT encrypt). DNS poisoning/spoofing attacks modify DNS cache.
DHCP server listens here. Client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER → server offers on 67. Exam trap: rogue DHCP server = MITM attack. Mitigate with DHCP snooping on switches.
DHCP client sends/receives on this port. DORA: Discover (client→255.255.255.255:67), Offer (server→client:68), Request, Acknowledge.
Trivial FTP. No auth, no encryption. Used for PXE boot, firmware updates, network device config backups. Exam trap: lightweight but insecure — restrict with ACLs, never use over untrusted networks.
Unencrypted web traffic. Exam trap: always redirect HTTP→HTTPS (443). A site accepting logins over port 80 is a vulnerability. Modern browsers mark HTTP as 'Not Secure'.

AD authentication protocol. Uses tickets (TGT, service tickets). Mutual authentication. Requires time sync (NTP port 123) — tickets expire if clock skew >5 min. Exam trap: Kerberos = AD auth, not LDAP.
Post Office Protocol v3. Downloads email, typically deletes from server. No multi-device sync. Unencrypted. Exam trap: POP3 downloads and removes; IMAP keeps on server. Secure version = POP3S (995).

Network Time Protocol. Syncs clocks. Critical for Kerberos (max 5-min skew), log accuracy, certificate validation. Exam trap: NTP amplification DDoS — attacker spoofs source IP, sends small query, server sends large response to victim.
Microsoft RPC endpoint mapper. Used by DCOM, WMI. Common attack vector (Blaster worm). Exam trap: block at perimeter firewall. If exposed, attackers can enumerate Windows services.
NetBIOS name resolution (NBNS). Legacy — replaces DNS for Windows names. Exam trap: NetBIOS should be disabled in modern environments. NBNS poisoning = MITM (responder tool attack).
NetBIOS datagram service. Connectionless communication. Legacy. Exam trap: block at firewall. Modern Windows uses direct SMB (445) instead.
NetBIOS session for legacy file/print sharing. Replaced by SMB direct (445). Exam trap: if both 139 and 445 are open, SMB can fall back to NetBIOS. Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP for security.

Internet Message Access Protocol. Keeps email on server. Supports folders, server-side search, multi-device sync. Unencrypted. Exam trap: IMAP allows reading without downloading; secure version = IMAPS (993).

SNMP agent queries. Network device monitoring. v1/v2c use community strings (plaintext 'public'/'private') — insecure. v3 adds encryption + auth. Exam trap: if scenario says 'SNMP community string', assume v1/v2c and answer: upgrade to v3.

SNMP asynchronous alerts from managed devices to NMS. Events: interface down, high CPU, temperature threshold. Exam trap: traps are sent FROM devices TO management station (reverse direction of 161 queries).

Border Gateway Protocol. Internet routing between ASes. TCP for reliable peering. Exam trap: BGP hijacking = attacker announces false routes. Mitigate with RPKI/ROA. More Network+ than Security+ but appears in architecture questions.

Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. Queries AD/OpenDirectory. Unencrypted. Exam trap: LDAP authentication sends BIND request with password in plaintext (unless using SASL). Secure version = LDAPS (636).

HTTP over TLS. Encrypted web. Cornerstone of web security. Exam trap: TLS handshake = ClientHello → ServerHello+Cert → KeyExchange → ChangeCipherSpec → Finished. Know TLS 1.2 vs 1.3 (1.3 removes insecure options, faster).

Server Message Block direct. Windows file/print sharing, remote admin. SMBv1 had EternalBlue (WannaCry 2017). Exam trap: disable SMBv1, use SMBv3 with encryption. SMB over QUIC (Win Server 2022+) uses 443.
SMTP over TLS/SSL. Encrypted email submission. Exam trap: 465 (implicit TLS) vs 587 (STARTTLS, explicit upgrade). Both are secure. IANA reassigned 465 to SMTPS; 587 is standard for submission.
Internet Key Exchange. Establishes IPsec VPN Security Associations (SAs). Phase 1 (IKE SA) → Phase 2 (IPsec SA). Exam trap: IKE uses UDP 500. If NAT is detected, switches to UDP 4500 (NAT-T).

System logging. Sends logs from devices to central server. Unencrypted — can leak sensitive data. Exam trap: use Syslog over TLS (6514) for secure transport. Standard format: facility, severity, timestamp, hostname, message.

Authenticated email submission from clients (MUA) to server (MSA). Uses STARTTLS. Exam trap: port 25 = server-to-server relay (unauthenticated). Port 587 = client submission with auth. CompTIA expects you to differentiate.
LDAP over TLS. Encrypted directory queries. Exam trap: LDAPS uses a dedicated port (636). Alternative is STARTTLS on port 389 — not all servers support it. For secure AD auth, prefer LDAPS.
FTP over TLS data channel. Used with FTPS control (990). Exam trap: FTPS = FTP+TLS (explicit or implicit). SFTP = SSH-based (port 22). Different protocols despite similar names.
FTP over TLS control channel. Implicit TLS — connection is encrypted from start. Exam trap: distinguish FTPS (FTP+TLS, ports 989/990) from SFTP (SSH-based, port 22).
IMAP over TLS. Secure email retrieval, keeps messages on server, multi-device sync encrypted. Exam trap: scenario says 'users need secure email on multiple devices' → IMAPS (993), not POP3S (995).
POP3 over TLS. Secure email retrieval. Download-and-delete model. Exam trap: POP3S does NOT sync across devices. If a user reads email on phone, it's gone from server — laptop won't see it.
Microsoft SQL Server default. Database queries. Exam trap: restrict with firewall, disable SA account, use encrypted connections. Common target for ransomware (SMB + MSSQL combo attacks).

Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol. VPN tunneling — no encryption by itself. Exam trap: L2TP MUST be combined with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec). PPTP (1723) is deprecated. L2TP/IPsec uses UDP 500 (IKE) + 4500 (NAT-T) + 1701.

Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol. Legacy Microsoft VPN. MPPE encryption (broken). Exam trap: PPTP is deprecated — known vulnerabilities (MS-CHAPv2 cracked). Replace with L2TP/IPsec, SSTP (443), or IKEv2.

RADIUS authentication. IETF AAA standard. Used by 802.1X, VPN, WPA-Enterprise. Only password encrypted in packet (not full payload). Exam trap: RADIUS uses UDP (unlike TACACS+ TCP). Port 1812 = auth, 1813 = accounting.
RADIUS accounting. Tracks session start/stop, data usage, duration. Exam trap: accounting is SEPARATE from auth. Must open both 1812 and 1813 for full AAA.
MySQL/MariaDB database. Exam trap: bind to 127.0.0.1 if local-only, disable remote root login, use TLS. Default creds (root/blank) are a common vulnerability.

Remote Desktop Protocol. Windows remote GUI. UDP improves performance (UDP-favored in Win 8+). Exam trap: top attacker target — BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708), brute force. Mitigate: NLA, account lockout, VPN, restrict by firewall.
IPsec NAT Traversal. Encapsulates IPsec ESP in UDP when NAT detected. Exam trap: if both peers are behind NAT, IPsec switches from UDP 500 to UDP 4500. Always open both 500 and 4500 for IPsec VPN.

Session Initiation Protocol. VoIP call signalling — setup, teardown. Unencrypted. Exam trap: SIP is signalling only (sets up the call). Media (audio) uses RTP/SRTP on dynamic ports. Secure SIP = SIPS (5061).
SIP over TLS. Encrypted VoIP signalling. Exam trap: SIP + TLS = SIPS. SRTP (not SIP) encrypts the actual voice stream. Both are needed for secure VoIP.

Virtual Network Computing. Cross-platform remote desktop (RFB protocol). No native encryption. Exam trap: VNC is unencrypted — tunnel through SSH or use VPN. Replace with RDP + NLA for Windows, SSH X11 for Linux.
Windows Remote Management over HTTP. PowerShell remoting, WS-Man. Unencrypted by default. Exam trap: 5985 (HTTP) vs 5986 (HTTPS). Always prefer 5986 for encrypted WinRM.

Windows Remote Management over HTTPS. Encrypted PowerShell remoting. Uses TLS. Replaces DCOM/PSExec for remote Windows admin. Exam trap: WinRM must be enabled and firewall-opened for remote PowerShell.
Encrypted syslog over TLS (RFC 5425). Replaces UDP 514 for secure logging. Exam trap: if compliance requires encrypted log transport, use 6514. Also need to configure logging server certificate.

Front: TCP vs UDP — When to use each?
Back: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered delivery, retransmission. Used for web (80/443), email (25/587), SSH (22). UDP: connectionless, faster, no retransmission. Used for DNS (53), DHCP (67/68), NTP (123), SNMP (161), VoIP/RTP, VPN (500/4500). Exam trap: DNS uses BOTH — UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers.

Front: Protocol Security Pairs — Insecure vs Secure?
Back: Know these pairs: Telnet(23)→SSH(22), HTTP(80)→HTTPS(443), FTP(20/21)→SFTP(22)/FTPS(990), POP3(110)→POP3S(995), IMAP(143)→IMAPS(993), SMTP(25)→SMTPS(465)/587, LDAP(389)→LDAPS(636), SNMPv1/v2(161)→SNMPv3(161), PPTP(1723)→L2TP/IPsec(1701/500), RDP(3389)→RDP+NLA+VPN. Exam trap: if a question asks 'which protocol should replace X', pick the encrypted version.
